key_insight: Microscopic residual impurities in wide-bandgap perovskite films act as degradation nucleation sites, and their density can be rapidly detected to predict early instability.
engineering_relevance: A fast, non-invasive microscopy-plus-ML screening workflow can pre-qualify perovskite films for scalable manufacturing and stability control in tandem solar cells.
method: Nano-FTIR and high-resolution optical/scanning probe microscopy to chemically identify impurities
Photo-stress experiments to map where degradation starts and how it propagates
Reflected-light microscopy with machine-learning image analysis for rapid impurity detection
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that higher impurity density correlates with accelerated early degradation, and the imaging framework detects and quantifies harmful impurities within seconds.
watch_item: Performance depends on robust image-model calibration and may require film-specific validation to avoid misclassifying benign microfeatures as harmful impurities.
paper_title: High-Throughput Imaging of Degradation-Inducing Microscopic Impurities in Perovskite Solar Cells
